name: Calligraphy Portrait
basis: calligram in a script font: letters grow and overlap in the darks (how)
note: Ink build-up is overlap of font glyphs; no nib or brush modelled. Arguable as partly (calligraphy).

lumenary.blurb: Flowing script in layers: the letters grow large and overlap on the dark parts, so the ink builds the tones.

facts.from: Calligraphic traditions of Europe, the Middle East and East Asia

why: A calligrapher builds tone with layers of ink. Here the letters swell and overlap in the dark parts of the picture, so they pile into black, and stay small and thin in the light parts, where the parchment shows between them. The whole portrait is made of one sentence and one idea: more letters on top of each other means darker.
how: Draw a parchment page with faint stains and a double ink border.
Letter the sentence in a flowing script on lines that rise or fall by the chosen slant.
Make letters very large and heavy where the picture is dark, and small and thin where it is light.
Advance each letter by only about 62 percent of its own width, so neighbours overlap and ink builds up.
Turn letters to follow the baseline with a tiny random wobble, and stamp an optional red seal.
history: Writing arranged into images is a long tradition. Greek poets shaped words into wings and altars more than two thousand years ago, and Persian and Ottoman calligraphers composed names and verses into the outlines of birds, boats and lions. Red seals, small stamps of a name, mark a finished work in many East Asian traditions.
terms: The angle at which letters lean from vertical.
A small stamp in red ink that signs a work.
paragraphs: The page is parchment (a radial gradient, a few faint stains) with a double border in ink. The sentence is then lettered in a flowing script on lines that rise or fall by the slant you choose. What makes it a portrait is that the letters change size: where the picture is dark they are very large and heavy, and since each letter only advances about 62% of its own width, neighbouring letters pile up on each other and the ink builds into black. In the light parts they are small and thin and the parchment shows between them.

Spaces advance by a fixed fraction of the size, and every letter is turned to follow the baseline with a tiny random wobble. The picture is stretched and blurred as in Handwritten, so the tones are smooth. An optional red seal, a rounded square with a pale inner frame and a single letter, is stamped in the bottom corner. Layering rather than drawing is the whole idea: tone comes from how many letters overlap, much as it does in an engraving.
